title: AI Video Generators for Clips and Creative Workflows
description: Explore AI video generators for scenes, explainers, and visual drafts, with guidance on input types, creative controls, revisions, and production fit.
introduction: AI video generators create moving visual material from text, images, scripts, or other supported inputs. This category spans scene generation and products that assemble a more complete video workflow. It differs from editing recorded footage, although a single product may do both. Start by deciding whether you need a new shot, an animated still, or a narrated sequence, because those outputs require different controls and levels of post-production work.
capabilities: Create moving visual drafts from the input types a product supports.
Explore shot composition, atmosphere, and motion through available generation controls.
Compare variations and continue selected clips where revision tools permit.
Move chosen footage into an editing workflow for a finished video.

audiences.label: Creative producers
audiences.text: Explore new shots or visual concepts before selecting material for a wider sequence and editorial review.

audiences.label: Business content teams
audiences.text: Prepare explainer or promotional drafts, checking the accuracy of the message and the work remaining before publication.

criteria.label: Output type
criteria.text: Distinguish generated scenes, avatar presentations, animated images, and assembled videos rather than comparing their previews as identical tasks.

criteria.label: Revision control
criteria.text: Test whether you can change one element, preserve a subject, or continue a shot without losing the chosen direction.

criteria.label: Production cost
criteria.text: Estimate usable footage after retries and editing, including resolution, duration, audio, and the applicable usage allowance.

workflow: Define the intended video, audience, and required shots, then identify which material must be generated and which already exists.
Generate short representative samples and inspect motion, subject consistency, text, and audio where relevant.
Select usable material, complete the edit, and review continuity, claims, and output requirements before sharing the finished video.

faqs.question: How is video generation different from video editing?
faqs.answer: Generation creates new moving material or assembles it from inputs. Editing reshapes existing footage. Many workflows need both, so compare the new material a tool produces and the editing steps still required.

faqs.question: Should I start from text or an image?
faqs.answer: Use text when exploring an unconstrained scene; an image can help establish the initial appearance of a subject or setting. Test the supported controls because a reference does not guarantee consistent motion or later frames.

faqs.question: How should I compare generation costs?
faqs.answer: Compare the cost of usable footage, including unsuccessful attempts, variations, and required output settings. A low per-generation price can be less informative than the budget needed to finish a representative scene.

faqs.question: Can a generated clip be considered a finished video?
faqs.answer: Sometimes a short clip is the intended deliverable, but longer work often needs sequencing, audio, titles, and continuity review. Inspect the complete viewer experience instead of assuming generation replaces every production step.

faqs.question: What should I inspect in a sample clip?
faqs.answer: Watch the entire clip for unstable subjects, inconsistent objects, awkward motion, and unintended text or audio. Check the required resolution and format, then repeat the test with another representative shot.
